newsitem.title: UK: RUGBY UNION-JOHNSON DETERMINED TO MAKE LIONS ROAR.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-JOHNSON DETERMINED TO MAKE LIONS ROAR.

text.p: Life just keeps getting better for Martin Johnson but he will consider his remarkable season a failure if the British Lions lose the forthcoming test series in South Africa.
After succeeding Dean Richards as Leicester captain in the winter, the formidable lock has risen to become the first Englishman to lead the Lions since Bill Beaumont in 1980.
And days after leading Leicester to the Pilkington Cup, his reputation was further enhanced on Thursday when he was crowned English rugby's player of the season.
Everything is now geared towards Lions success and the 27-year-old Johnson will fly out with the rest of the 35-strong playing party in confident mood.
"If I didn't think we could win the test series, I'd stay at home and go on holiday," he said. "It's a massive task but the pleasure of being a Lion will be doubled if we can be winning Lions."

The first post World War Two Lions captain never to have led his own country, Johnson nevertheless has the full backing of management and players alike. All are united in their desire to win the series.
"We have just got to do whatever we have to do to win the test series. If that means playing 15-man rugby, then great, if it means playing another way, then so be it."

No stranger to southern hemisphere rugby, having represented New Zealand Colts during an 18-month visit in the early 1990s, Johnson also had a close-up view of South Africa during England's tour there in 1994 and the 1995 World Cup.
But if hard pitches and big opposition mean a faster, more confrontational game the Lions are ready for it. "If it's a faster game than we're used to, we've just got to get used to it very quickly."
Johnson has developed into a world-class player at Leicester and under the guiding eye of former Wallaby coach Bob Dwyer has grown r in stature this season.
"He thinks clearly when the pressure is on and doesn't shirk any responsibilities himself," said Dwyer. "He's also one of the really, really tough people in the game."
One of the few automatic choices for the test team, Johnson is aware of the tough challenge posed by the provincial sides exposed to the high-quality Super 12 series.
But the captain will have played more than 50 matches by the time he lines up for the first test in Cape Town on June 21 and admits his gruelling schedule has taken its toll.
"It has been a long hard season, that's undeniable but I have never felt as good at the end of a season before. And there's a buzz about this squad."
The Lions have spent a week of "recovery and regeneration" in southern England, developing as a squad and building their fitness with a plethora of non-rugby activities.
Despite his dour, no-nonsense demeanour, Johnson is clearly excited by what lies ahead.
"It's a one-off opportunity," he said. "If we can go to South Africa and win a test series, it would be the pinnacle of a lot of the guys' careers. It really is that major."
